claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic CoCrFeNi with a homogeneous single-phase FCC microstructure.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Ti to CoCrFeNi will induce finely dispersed nanoprecipitates.
Melting followed by a precipitation-promoting heat treatment will produce nanoprecipitates and grain refinement in CoCrFeNi-Ti.
The Ti-modified alloy will develop a dual-phase nanohierarchical structure containing nano-coupled grains and uniformly dispersed nanoprecipitates.
A nanohierarchical architecture of nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates can provide adaptive friction-interface protection from room temperature to 800 °C.
At lower temperatures, the fine structure will relax frictional stress through multiple deformation pathways.
The grain-boundary and nanoprecipitate network will distribute frictional stress and inhibit severe plastic deformation at room temperature.
Stress distribution and suppression of severe plastic deformation will lower room-temperature friction.
At elevated temperature, nanoprecipitates will promote timely formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer.
Ti-rich nanoprecipitates in CoCrFeNi-Ti will oxidize to form the nanocrystalline glaze layer.
A dense nanocrystalline glaze layer will minimize adhesive and oxidative wear at about 800 °C.
Glaze-layer formation will maintain low friction at high temperature.
The Ti-alloyed variant will have a lower average coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The Ti-alloyed variant will have a wear rate up to one to two orders of magnitude lower than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The proposed operating boundary is sliding in ambient air from room temperature to 800 °C under normal loads of approximately 5–20 N.
The hypothesis does not claim applicability outside the stated temperature range or in highly aggressive chemical environments.
Interactions between Ti and the other alloying elements during prolonged high-temperature exposure may affect long-term stability.
